title: Phosphatidic acid phosphatase PAP2-2 controls lipid metabolism and membrane homeostasis in Leishmania mexicana.

abstract: Developing broadly protective influenza vaccines remains a major challenge for global public health. Influenza B viruses cause about one-third of all annual influenza virus infections and current vaccines only show moderate effectiveness against matched virus strains, therefore, development of more effective and broadly protective vaccines against them is important. Chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinin (cHA and mHA) immunogens are under investigation as broadly protective influenza B vaccine candidates. The lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated nucleoside-modified mRNA technology has recently revolutionized vaccination and gained widespread interest due to its successful use in the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Here, we evaluated influenza B cHA and mHA mRNA-LNP vaccines in non-human primates and compared their immunogenicity to a quadrivalent seasonal influenza virus vaccine. mHA mRNA-LNPs induced high binding antibody titers against antigenically distant influenza B virus strains, with significant hemagglutination inhibition and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity activity and provided protection in mice in a serum transfer challenge experiment. This approach shows great promise for developing broadly protective influenza B vaccines.

title: Mosaic Hemagglutinin-Based Influenza B mRNA-LNP Vaccine Induces Strong Humoral Immune Response in Non-Human Primates.

abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most severe manifestation of acute lung injury (ALI), characterized by diffuse pulmonary inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and high morbidity and mortality. Despite the clinical significance of ARDS, no effective pharmacological therapies are currently available. In this study, we developed a lung-targeted mRNA-sulfonium lipid nanoparticle (mRNA/sLNP) delivery system for the treatment of ALI/ARDS in a mouse model. We first examined different heads and tails to optimize sulfonium lipid structure, leading to the identification of a top-performing HOSEH formulation. HOSEH sLNP was comprehensively characterized and subsequently loaded with interleukin-10 (IL-10) mRNA, an immunomodulatory cytokine with potent anti-inflammatory activity. As a proof-of-concept, in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI mouse model, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP demonstrated both prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, significantly attenuating pulmonary and systemic inflammation, restoring alveolar-capillary barrier integrity, and reducing lung tissue damage. These findings highlight the potential of lung-targeted mRNA therapeutics in inflammatory lung diseases. With further development, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of ALI and ARDS.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron loss. Aberrant RNA metabolism is one of its most consistent molecular features, and ALS has long been framed as a disease of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), given that mutations in RBPs are among the most frequent genetic causes of ALS. However, a growing number of ALS-associated genes encode proteins that lack canonical RNA-binding domains; nonetheless, their mutations also disrupt RNA homeostasis. This review examines how these non-canonical disease modulators perturb RNA metabolism. We group these factors into three functional classes. One includes proteostasis regulators, whose dysfunction impairs protein quality control and promotes the accumulation of aggregation-prone RBPs in cytoplasmic inclusions and persistent stress granules. Another involves factors that elicit RNA toxicity or disrupt ribonucleoprotein organization, including GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9ORF72 and CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1. The third class comprises factors governing axonal RNA granule transport. Across these categories, a shared consequence is the disruption of mRNA processing, stability, localization, and translation in motor neurons. We further discuss how epitranscriptomic dysregulation, particularly altered m6A and m1A modification states, may contribute to ALS pathology. We also discuss the therapeutic implications of this mechanistic convergence in defective RNA metabolism in ALS.

abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1 Δ mutants lack β-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

abstract: Gene therapy is one of the breakthrough strategies for treating genetically acquired and complicated disorders owing to its potential in regulating the expression of genes precisely. Nevertheless, the success of any gene therapy will depend upon the development of a safe and efficient system for gene delivery. Nanotechnology has brought about great changes in the field of non-viral gene delivery systems by providing carriers that increase stability, facilitate cellular uptake, allow endosomal escape, and have tissue specificity without causing systemic toxicity. This review examines the basic concepts underlying the design of nanocarriers for the delivery of plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and the CRISPR-Cas genome editing system. The current review provides an overview of different viral and non-viral delivery platforms for plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing systems. The discussion focuses on adenoviral, adeno-associated viral, lentiviral, retroviral, herpes simplex viral and virus-like particle delivery platforms, as well as non-viral nanocarriers. The review further highlights clinically validated examples, such as liposomal nanoparticles used for the delivery of RNA-based therapies and discusses some of the translational challenges that still exist in terms of transfection efficiency, long-term safety issues, manufacturability at a large scale, and regulatory acceptance. Finally, some of the latest trends in gene delivery, such as artificial intelligence-assisted nanoparticle design, smart multi-responsive nanoparticles, and personalized nanomedicine, have been outlined as the most important driving forces in developing the next generation of gene delivery technologies.

abstract: Chronic pulmonary diseases are often associated with high morbidity and/or mortality, and many lack effective therapies. Direct delivery of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to the lung shows promise for the treatment of pulmonary diseases. Despite their overall low risk profiles, systemically delivered ASOs can be associated with pro-inflammatory responses including activation of the alternative complement pathway, particularly near administration sites. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) and Beagle dogs have both been used in ASO toxicity studies, but comparative suitability of these species for ASO safety assessment has not been established. Herein, we compare the tolerability of a phosphorothioate (PS) gapmer ASO in these species after dosing with a nebulized ASO delivered by inhalation at 15 mg/kg once weekly for 13 weeks via face mask. Although lung concentrations of ASO were similar in cynomolgus monkeys and Beagle dogs, ASO inhalation was associated with greater pro-inflammatory responses in the monkey. Anti-drug antibody production, C-reactive protein elevation, complement activation, increased bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cellularity, increased lung weights, and microscopic evidence of pulmonary inflammation were present in the monkey but not the dog. Therefore, although NHPs and dogs can be used in toxicity testing of inhaled ASOs, NHPs exhibit a predisposition to complement activation and development of pulmonary inflammation.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 620,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli . Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors.

abstract: Rare genetic diseases affect over 350 million patients worldwide and have long posed significant challenges in modern medicine. Although messenger RNA (mRNA) was initially considered unsuitable due to its instability, immunogenicity, and inability to cross biological barriers, the COVID-19 pandemic established mRNA as a clinically validated therapeutic. Advances in mRNA synthesis and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) design have since improved stability, translation, safety, and scalability, offering a modern strategy, alongside advances in our understanding of rare diseases. By enabling the production of functional proteins without modifying the genome, mRNA-LNP offer a flexible solution to restore proteins lost through rare genetic diseases. Despite this promise, their application for rare genetic diseases remains at early stages, with most candidates in preclinical developments or early Phase 1/2 trials. This review underlines recent advances in mRNA-based protein replacement for rare genetic disorders, integrating innovations in mRNA design combined with LNPs optimization. It also discusses current challenges, emerging innovations, and future perspectives. While early clinical programs have mainly targeted liver-based disorders, the field is expanding toward pulmonary, hematologic, and neuromuscular diseases. Continued multidisciplinary efforts may establish mRNA nanotherapies as a transformative treatment option for patients with rare genetic disorders.

abstract: Epigenetic regulation controls transcriptional programs that govern cortical neurogenesis. Here, we present a protocol for locus-specific manipulation of histone acetylation using a CRISPR-dCas9-Kat2a epigenome-editing system. As an example, we describe the design and validation of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs), assembly of a Cre-dependent all-in-one CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) vector, validation of promoter-specific H3K9 acetylation in Neuro2A cells, and targeted delivery of epigenome-editing constructs into the embryonic mouse cortex by in utero electroporation (IUE). For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Sokpor et al.1 and Kerimoglu et al.2.

abstract: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

abstract: Spatial and temporal organisation of membrane-associated components is fundamental to cellular signalling, yet remains difficult to engineer in minimal synthetic systems. In synthetic cells, DNA and RNA nanotechnology offer programmable molecular organisation at membranes, while in vitro transcription (IVT) enables gene expression-driven regulation. However, integrating these systems within cell-like compartments, such as giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), remains challenging due to undesirable interactions between transcription machinery and nucleic acid assemblies. Here, we present a modular strategy that couples in situ RNA production to dynamic DNA localisation at GUV synthetic cell membranes. RNA strands, transcribed within GUVs, function as linkers that recruit DNA-conjugated cargo to lipid membranes, enabling programmable spatial organisation. Using this framework, we achieved reversible membrane localisation through toehold-mediated strand displacement and RNase H-mediated degradation. This work establishes a gene expression-driven platform for programmable and dynamic control of membrane-associated components in synthetic cells, providing a foundation for constructing dynamic signalling assemblies and higher-order cellular behaviours.

abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: This study is intended to confirm the efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetic (PK) profile, and the durability of hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg) suppression observed with bepirovirsen for 24 weeks (with loading doses) as compared to the placebo arm. This study will have 4 stages: a) Double-blind treatment (bepirovirsen or placebo) for 24 weeks. b) Nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment for 24 weeks. c) NA cessation stage OR Continue NA for 24 weeks. d) Durability of response and follow up for further 24 weeks for participants who stopped NA treatment at Week 48. The arms will be stratified based on HBsAg level (HBsAg greater than or equal to \[≥\] 100 international unit per milliliter \[IU/mL\] to less than or equal \[≤\]1000 IU/mL or greater than \[\>\] 1000 IU/mL to ≤3000 IU/mL) at screening. The total duration of the study, including screening (up to 60 days), the double-blind treatment stage (24 weeks), the On NA only stage (24 weeks), and the NA cessation and durability stages (48 weeks) is up to approximately 104 weeks at maximum for each participant.

abstract: A theophylline-binding RNA aptamer has been extensively studied as a model for RNA-ligand interactions. While previous structural analyses have provided insights into its binding mechanism, the precise nature of ligand recognition remains unclear. In this study, we present a crystal structure of a novel ligand-free conformation of the theophylline aptamer. Unlike previously reported ligand-free conformations within Fab-RNA complexes, the ligand-binding region adopts a well-organized structure in which the space occupied by theophylline in the ligand-bound state is instead filled by an RNA nucleotide. Structural evaluation with a residue-separation-based statistical potential revealed that the newly identified ligand-free conformation shows greater consistency with statistically preferred intramolecular atomic arrangements than the other ligand-bound and ligand-free conformations examined. These findings provide new insights into the conformational landscape underlying theophylline recognition.

abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. This review explores its advantages over flowering plants traditionally used more often for biotechnology, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and maize, including shorter life cycles and ease to handle experimentally, being haploid, and much higher efficiency for integration of transgenes into its genome by homologous recombination. In addition, Physco's ability to maintain episomes also introduces an additional possibility for transgene expression and manipulation. With these advantageous traits, Physco has already been used for synthetic genomes, recombinant protein production, metabolic engineering and artificial organelle engineering. These applications have been enabled by various toolkits developed for construction of transformation cassettes, DNA and RNA editing, as well as different reporters to allow microscopy imaging or quantification of gene expression. While Physco does have limitations, such as its high number of duplicated genes which can present issues when tweaking of native genes is involved, these certainly do not prevent Physco becoming a useful synthetic biology model for further applications on Earth and future space explorations.

abstract: Ardisia gigantifolia Stapf, belonging to the genus Ardisia (Primulaceae), is an important traditional medicinal plant with extensive applications in folk medicine. However, its mitochondrial genome remains unexplored. The first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia was sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and Oxford Nanopore Technologies platforms and assembled using a hybrid strategy implemented in Unicycler. The genome was assembled into a 639,756 bp circular configuration with a GC content of 42.02%. ONT long reads supported the contig connections within this configuration, although alternative configurations may also exist. The mitochondrial genome contained 38 protein-coding genes, 20 tRNA genes, and 3 rRNA genes. Repetitive sequence analysis identified abundant repeat elements, including 63 simple sequence repeats, 62 tandem repeats, and 73 dispersed repeat regions, which may contribute to mitochondrial genome expansion and structural complexity. In addition, 72 mitochondrial plastid DNA fragments were identified between the mitochondrial and plastid genomes. A total of 451 C-to-U RNA editing sites were predicted across 38 protein-coding genes using Deepred-Mt. Fourteen editing sites in nad4L, including the conversion of its ACG start codon to AUG, and a stop-codon editing site in ccmFC were experimentally validated. Phylogenetic analysis supported a close relationship between A. gigantifolia and Aegiceras corniculatum. This study reports the first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia, providing a valuable genomic resource for understanding mitochondrial genome evolution, phylogenetic relationships, and molecular characteristics of Ardisia.

abstract: This is a 2-part, phase 1/2, open-label, multicenter study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacogenomics, and efficacy of THT40 administered orally daily. This study consists of Phase 1 and Phase 2 components in subjects with advanced solid tumors and lymphoma with a focus on tumors with ARID1A and similar mutations who have progressed despite having received standard therapy or for whom no standard therapy exists.
description:
Phase 1 part of the study will consist of a dose-escalation and a dose-finding component. Phase 1 also includes expansion cohorts for subject with ARID1A and similar mutations.

Phase 2 will enroll subjects with locally advanced, recurrent, or metastatic, histologically confirmed advanced solid tumors or lymphoma, who have failed all standard therapies or for whom standard therapy does not exist, into 8 groups:

Group 1: Bladder cancer

Group 2: Breast cancer: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)

Group 3: Lung cancer (non-small cell lung cancer \[NSCLC\] and small cell lung cancer \[SCLC\])

Group 4: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and biliary tract cancer (BTC)

Group 5: Metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) including KRAS-mutated mCRC

Group 6: B-cell lymphoma including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)

Group 7: T-cell lymphoma (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma \[CTCL\] and peripheral T-cell lymphoma \[PTCL\])

Group 8: Basket cohort: tumor types that are suspected to have a related mechanism of action but are not included in previous groups including, esophageal, prostate, ovarian and pancreatic cancers

abstract:
Beyond pulmonary complications, COPD presents with extrapulmonary manifestations including reduced cognitive, cardiovascular, and muscle function. While exercise training is the cornerstone in the non-pharmacological treatment of COPD, there is a need for new exercise training methods.

The COPD-HIIT trial intend to investigate the effects and mechanisms of 12 weeks supramaximal high-intensity interval-training (HIIT) compared to moderate intensive continous training (MICT) in people with COPD and matched healthy controls on important clinical outcomes.

The trial also intends to compare the effects of 24 months of exercise training (supramaximal HIIT or MICT) to usual care in people with COPD on brain health, cardiorespiratory fitness and muscle power; in people with COPD.

description:
COPD-HIIT is a prospective, multi-centre, randomised, controlled, parallel-group superiority trial with assessor and data analyst blinding, featuring a 1:1 allocation ratio and two separate phases. In Phase 1, the trial will investigate the effects and mechanisms of a 12 week intervention with supramaximal HIIT compared to MICT in people with COPD and matched healthy controls. Upon completing the initial 12 week intervention and follow-up assessments, people with COPD, but not healthy controls, will enter Phase 2 of the trial. Phase 2 comprises a 21 month maintenance exercise program. Subsequently, exercise training (supramaximal HIIT or MICT) will be performed until a 24 month follow-up. A separate control group of people with COPD, receiving usual care only, will undergo assessments at baseline and 24-months, making Phase 2 a partially randomized controlled trial.

The primary objectives are:

1. to determine and compare the effect of 12-weeks of supramaximal HIIT and MICT on cognitive function, cardiorespiratory fitness, and muscle power in people with COPD compared to matched healthy controls (Phase 1).
2. to determine and compare the effect of 24-months of supramaximal HIIT, MICT and usual care on cognitive function, cardiorespiratory fitness and muscle power in people with COPD (Phase 2).

Phase 1 and 2 of the COPD-HIIT project will be performed at two recruiting centres. 1) Department of Community Medicine and Rehabilitation, Physiotherapy, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden and Norrlands Universitetssjukhus, and 2) Faculty of Rehabilitation Sciences, Hasselt University, Diepenbeek, Belgium and Ziekenhuis Oost-Limburg (ZOL, Genk, Belgium).

In Phase 1, eligible participants will be randomized to either supramaximal HIIT (intervention arm) or MICT (active control arm) on a stationary bicycle (Smart ZBike, Zycle, Valencia, Spain). For both arms, training is performed two to three times per week for a total of 30 sessions (Table 1) using a group format with groups of 4-8 participants at the same time. Both protocols enable controlled and systematic adjustments of training intensity by means of standardized criteria to achieve a progressive overload

Regarding supramaximal HIIT, importantly, while the intensity is supramaximal, it is dosed and performed at a given fraction of the maximum capacity that the person can produce during the bout (6-seconds). In contrast to an all-out regimen, or sprint interval training (SIT), this allows for the introduction and titration of intensity to the highest acceptable level without the individual feeling unwell during the process.

In Phase 2, participants with COPD will enter a 21 month maintenance phase. They will continue to exercise using the same training modality (HIIT or MICT) as during the first 12-weeks but can select between three different settings to continue their training: "Home", "Outpatient", or "Mix" setting. Notably, the participant can, at any time during the maintenance period, change between the "Home", "Outpatient" or "Mix" settings when conducting their endurance training. Irrespective of the originally assigned group (supramaximal HIIT or MICT) or if the participant selects to continue in "Home", "Outpatient" or "Mix" setting, they will also perform a resistance training (RT) regime. The RT regime will consist of ten lower and upper-body exercises designed following American College of Sports Medicine guidelines and other relevant RT literature for increasing muscular strength, endurance, and power.

All exercise sessions will be held and supervised by an experienced health care professional, such as physiotherapists, exercise physiologists or other health professional with equivalent expertise. All intervention providers will receive training on exercise intervention protocols to ensure standardization among centres.

The between-group effects will be analyzed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). In the ANCOVA, baseline values, age, sex, center and VO2peak will be used as covariates. There will be one model for the COPD group and one for HC. To investigate any differential effects to the interventions between COPD and HC, an additional model including the Group (COPD/HC) × Intervention (HIIT/MICT) will be performed. Furthermore, pre-specified longitudinal mediation analyses will be performed on the entire MRI and PET/CT sample between changes in VO2peak, neurodegenerative measures, e.g., cognitive function and hippocampal volume, and inflammation levels between baseline and 24 months.

Analyses will employ the intention-to-treat when applicable. Meaning that all participants randomized, whether they receive their allocated intervention or withdrew from the trial, will be included in the analysis. The primary analyses are performed using Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) for missing data. The imputation will be done separately for each intervention arm. In addition, a per-protocol analysis (defined as \> 75% attendance rate as well as no exacerbations during the last two weeks prior to follow-up assessment), and a complete-case analysis (including participants with complete outcome measurements independent on attendance rate) will be reported.

The full study protocol adheres to the SPIRIT guidelines and its outcomes extension, with intervention descriptions further guided by the TIDieR checklist the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template (CERT). Publications from COPD-HIIT will follow the CONSORT statement, or relevant guidelines at the time of publication. Publications including qualitative outcomes will also be guided by the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ).

outcomes.description: Global cognitive function will be assessed as the Z-score determined by the combined performances on six tests from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) and the trail making test (TMT-A, TMT-B). The following tests from the CANTAB will be used: Motor screening task, reaction time, visual information processing, paired associates learning, spatial working memory, verbal recognition memory. The test battery takes around 60 minutes to complete. The test scores from the seven tests will be combined into a composite Z-score. The Z-score describes how much a point deviates from a mean or specific point. The Z-score represents how many standard deviations an individual's score is from the mean score of the reference population, which is represented as zero.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline global cognitive function

outcomes.description: Measured as maximum oxygen uptake (VO2peak \[ml O2/min/kg\]) during a standardized ramp-protocol cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) on a cycle ergometer. The CPET will start with a 3-minute resting phase before a 3-minute unloaded (or lowest wattage possible) warm-up phase. The aim is to have a ramp-phase of 8-12 minutes, until the participant stops due to voluntarily exhaustion, symptom-limitation or failure to maintain a cadence of 50-70 RPM.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cardiorespiratory fitness

outcomes.description: Peak power (Nm/s) assessed during a seated leg extension in a dymanometer (Biodex System 4). Participants will be instructed to extend their leg as fast and as hard as possible and then passively return the leg to the starting position.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline quadriceps muscle power

outcomes.description: Assessed using standard MRI-sequences including in a 3 Tesla MRI-scanner. T1-weighted images will be used to determine volumes of grey matter, white matter and lateral ventricle size. T2-weighted, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and susceptibility weighted (SW) images are collected to assess perivascular spaces, lacunes, white-matter lesions and microbleeds. For structural MRI data volume (mm3), area (mm2) and cortical thickness (mm) will be the unit of measure.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline brain structure

outcomes.description: Task-based functional MRI will be performed to evaluate brain activity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, measured as BOLD signal change.The face-name association task will be used.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline brain activity

outcomes.description: Assessed using arterial spin labelling (ASL) in a 3T MRI-scanner (mL/100g/minute).
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cerebral perfusion

outcomes.description: In vivo neuroinflammation is measured as uptake rate (ki) of 11C-deprenyl in the brain assessed with PET/CT (General Electric, WI, USA) under resting-state conditions after intravenous injection of 314 MBq of 11C-Deprenyl. . Uptake rate of 11C-deprenyl in the brain is modeled with Patlak analyses, where higher uptake is representative of higher levels of inflammation.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline neuroinflammation

outcomes.description: Test duration (mm:ss) on a constant-workload cycle test (CWRT) set at 75% of maximal power achieved during a CPET. After a 3-minute resting phase and a 3-minute warm-up phase at 30% of MAP, participants will cycle at a constant workload corresponding to 75% of MAP with a self-selected pedaling cadence of 50-70 RPM. Participants will be instructed to exercise for as long as possible.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline exercise tolerance

outcomes.description: A intermediate test at 6-weeks will be done to regulate training intensity and the result will be used as a secondary outcome. Measured as maximum oxygen uptake (VO2peak \[ml O2/min/kg\]) during a standardized ramp-protocol cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) on a cycle ergometer. The CPET will start with a 3-minute resting phase before a 3-minute unloaded (or lowest wattage possible) warm-up phase. The aim is to have a ramp-phase of 8-12 minutes, until the participant stops due to voluntarily exhaustion, symptom-limitation or failure to maintain a cadence of 50-70 RPM.
outcomes.measure: Change from cardiorespiratory fitness

outcomes.description: Capillary blood lactate (mmol/L) will be measured during and immediately after the CWRT to assess the metabolic demand.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline lactate concentration during constant-workload cycle test (CWRT)

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB Motor screen task. During the test, colored crosses appear in different locations on the screen. The participant must select the cross as quickly and accurately as possible.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Motor screening task

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB reaction time test. During the test, participants must select a button on the screen. Circles are presented above the button and the participant is asked to react as soon as possible once a yellow dot appears in one of the circles by clicking the corresponding circle.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Reaction time

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB Visual information processing test. During the test, a white box is shown in the center of the screen where digits from 2 to 9 appear in a pseudo-random order at the rate of 100 digits per minute. Participants are requested to detect target sequences of digits (e.g., 2-4-6, 3-5-7, 4-6-8). When the participant sees the target sequence, they must respond by selecting the button in the center of the screen as quickly as possible.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Visual information processing

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB Paired associates learning test. In the test, boxes are displayed on the screen and are opened in a randomized order. One or more of them will contain a pattern. The patterns are then displayed in the middle of the screen, one at a time and the participant must select the box in which the pattern was originally located.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Paired associates learning

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB spatial working memory test. During the test, several colored boxes are shown on the screen. The aim of this test is that, by selecting the boxes and using a process of elimination, the participant should find one yellow 'token' in each of several boxes and use them to fill up an empty column on the right-hand side of the screen
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Spatial working memory

outcomes.description: Test score in the trail making test. The TMT consists of two parts, A and B and is performed with paper and pencil. During part A, the participant needs to connect 25 digits in ascending order as fast as possible by drawing lines between the digits. During part B, the participants need to connect 13 digits in ascending order and 12 letters in alphabetical order, alternating digits, and letters (i.e., 1 - A - 2 - B - 3 - C, etcetera) as fast as possible by drawing lines between the digits and letters.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Executive function

outcomes.description: Intensity (produced power, in watts) at the final stage during a Borg cycle strength test (BCST). The BCST is a submaximal cycle ergometer test that is used to estimate maximum mean power output for 30 seconds (MPO30) without an all-out effort. The BCST consists of 30-second efforts with increasing intensity, interspersed with 30-seconds passive recovery between each effort. With a target pedaling cadence of 80-90 RPM, participants cycle until they score an RPE of ≥17, or when they cannot keep the target cadence (\<75 RPM for five seconds).
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline anaerobic exercise capacity

outcomes.description: Test score in the CANTAB verbal recognition memory test. During the test, the participant is shown a list of words to remember. During the recognition phase, the participant is asked to say whether they remember seeing the word on the screen before. The word can be one of the originals, or a new word (distractor) which they have not yet seen before.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline cognitive function: Verbal recognition memory

outcomes.description: Levels of hs-CRP in venous blood. Unit of measure is mg/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline chronic inflammation

outcomes.description: Llevels of interleukin-6, interleukin-8 and TNF-alpha in venous blood. Unit of measure is pq/mL.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline inflammatory markers

outcomes.description: Plasma levels of fibrinogen. Unit of measure is g/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline fibrinogen

outcomes.description: White blood cells and eosinophils measured in whole blood. Unit of measure is count x 10\^9/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline blood cell count

outcomes.description: Levels of BDNF, irisin, IGF-1, Cathepsin B and clusterin in venous blood samples. Unit of measure is pq/ml.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline neurotrophic factors

outcomes.description: Concentration of lactate in capillary blood samples. Unit of measure is mmol/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline resting lactate

outcomes.description: Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, non-HDL and triglycerides. Unit of measure is mmol/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline blood lipid profile

outcomes.description: Plasma levels of glucose in fasted venous blood sample. Unit of measure is mmol/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline metabolic function: Glucose

outcomes.description: Plasma levels of insulin in fasted venous blood sample. Unit of measure is mIU/L.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline metabolic function: Insulin

outcomes.description: Levels of glucose and insulin levels will be used to calculate the HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance). The unit of measure is arbitrary units where values above 1.9 indicates early insulin resistance, and above 2.9 indicates significant insulin resistance.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline metabolic function: Insulin resistance

outcomes.description: Levels of Hb1Ac, measured as a percentage (%) of red blood cells that is bound to glucose.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline metabolic function: Glycated hemoglobin

outcomes.description: Muscle strength will be determined as the one-repetition maximum (1-RM) defined as the maximum torque (Nm/s) able to be lifted through the full range of motion during seated leg extension in the dominant leg, using a dymanometer (Biodex System 4)
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline quadriceps muscle strength

outcomes.description: Defined as the maximum number of repetitions able to be lifted with a good technique through the full ROM at an intensity corresponding to 45% of 1-RM, during seated leg extension in the dominant leg, using a dymanometer (Biodex System 4).
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline quadriceps muscle endurance

outcomes.description: Time needed (in seconds) to complete the 5-STS.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline functional performance: Five time sit-to-stand test (5-STS)

outcomes.description: Time needed (in seconds) to ascent a 10-step flight of stairs.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline functional performance: Stair climbing power test

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with morphometric analyses to determine cross-sectional fiber area of all fibres and per subtype. Unit of measurement is square micrometers.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline muscle fibre size

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with immunohistochemistry techniques to categorize fiber types. Expressed as relative distribution in percent and relative area of the muscle in percent.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline proportion of slow and fast subtypes of contractile myosin heavy chain isoforms

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with morphometric analysis to determine capillary density, estimated as the total number of capillaries per millimeter squared muscle cross-section.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline capillary density

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with morphometric analysis to determine the number of capillaries in close contact with each muscle fiber. Unit of measure is number of capillaries in close contact with fibre.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline capillaries per fiber

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with morphometric analysis to determine the number of capillaries around each fiber relative to its cross-sectional area.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline capillaries to fiber area

outcomes.description: The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with morphometric analysis to determine the capillary-to-fiber ratio
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline capillaries sharing factor

outcomes.description: Staining of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-tetrazolium reductase, succinate dehydrogenase, and cytochrome c oxidase. Measured as % of fibers with abnormal staining pattern and fiber area in µm2 of fibers with abnormal staining pattern.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline myofiber and mitochondrial disruption/abnormalities (NADH-TR)

outcomes.description: mRNA and protein levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 (PGC-1) alpha and PGC-1beta. Unit of measure is fold-change or arbitrary units.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline mitochondrial biogenesis

outcomes.description: Enzyme activities of phosphofructokinase (PFK; glycolysis), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; anaerobic glycolysis), citrate synthase (CSM Krebs cycle), succinate dehydrogenase (SDH; Krebs cycle), 3-hydroxyacyl Coenzyme A dehydrogenase (HADH; beta-oxidation) and mitochondrial complex I-V. Unit of measure is micromol/min/g tissue.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline enzyme activity

outcomes.description: Enzyme content of phosphofructokinase (PFK; glycolysis), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; anaerobic glycolysis), citrate synthase (CS; Krebs cycle), succinate dehydrogenase (SDH; Krebs cycle), 3-hydroxyacyl Coenzyme A dehydrogenase (HADH; beta-oxidation) and mitochondrial complex I-V. Unit of measure is micromol/min/g tissue.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline enzyme content

outcomes.description: mRNA and protein level of VEGF (fold change or arbitrary units).
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline angiogenesis

outcomes.description: mRNA and protein level of BDNF, fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) and kynurenine aminotransferase (KAT1-4). Unit of measure is fold change and arbitrary units.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline proteins related to muscle-brain cross talk

outcomes.description: Resting heart rate variability measured in the time domain as the root mean square of the successive differences (RMSSD, in milliseconds), and time domain (LH:HF ratio) using a chest strap heart rate monitor.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline modulation of autonomic cardic function

outcomes.description: Resting blood pressure, measured as systolic and diastolic pressure in mmHg.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline blood pressure

outcomes.description: Samples will be analysed for genome-wide DNA methylation, via the EPICarray technology.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline epigenetic modifications in muscle samples

outcomes.description: Whole blood EDTA samples will be analysed for genome-wide DNA methylation, via the EPICarray technology.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline epigenetic modifications in blood samples

outcomes.description: Body composition measures include body mass index, waist and hip circumference (cm), percentage of body fat, fat-free mass (kg), and fat-free mass index (kg/m2). Fatmass and fatfree mass is measured with bioelectrical impedance.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline body composition

outcomes.description: Measured vid the COPD Assessment Test (CAT)
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline impact of COPD in daily life
outcomes.time_frame: Baseline, 12 weeks, 6 months, 12 months, 15 months, 18 months, 21 months and 24 months

outcomes.description: Measured with the chronic respiratory disease questionnaire (COPD group only). The CRQ measures the impact of chronic respiratory disease on HRQoL and covers four key domains of HRQoL, including: dyspnea, fatigue, emotional function, and mastery. Each item is scored on a 7-point Likert scale; scores within each domain are summated for a total score per domain.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline disease specific quality of life
outcomes.time_frame: Baseline, 12 weeks, 6 months, 12 months, 15 months, 18 months, 21 months and 24 months

outcomes.description: Measured with the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire.It assesses an individual's HRQoL in five dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression91. Each dimension has five response levels, ranging from level 1 (no problems) to level 5 (extreme problems). By combining one level from each dimension, a health state ranging from 11111 (the best health state) to 55555 (the worst health state) is defined and converted into an index score using a scoring algorithm.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline Health related quality of life

outcomes.description: The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) will be used to assess states of depression and anxiety. The HADS is a reliable 14-item questionnaire regarding feeling of depression and anxiety in the past week which can be answered within 2 - 5 minutes. A separate score is given for depression and anxiety. where a higher score means higher severity.
outcomes.measure: Change from baseline state of depression and anxiety

outcomes.description: Self-perceived change in outcomes will be measured via the Global Rate of Change scale with the purpose to quantify the extent to which a participant's outcomes have improved or deteriorated over time. Participants will provide an answer via a 11-point Likert scale (-5 = "Much worse"; 0 = "Unchanged"; 5 = "Much better").
outcomes.measure: Self-percieved change

outcomes.description: Total amount of responders, defined as a response over the known minimal detectable change or minimal important difference for included tests, will be determined, and compared between HIIT and MICT.
outcomes.measure: Number of responders

outcomes.description: Completion rate is determined by the total number of participants still performing the exercise training intervention at 12-week and 24-month follow-up. Reasons for non-completion are also obtained.
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Completion rate

outcomes.description: Attendance rate is determined by the total number of attended sessions divided by total number of sessions prescribed, presented as a percentage. Reasons for non-attendance are also obtained.
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Attendance rate

outcomes.description: Exercise fidelity is determined as the incidence of exercise sessions requiring modifications, defined as any deviation from the prescribed exercise.
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Exercise fidelity

outcomes.description: Adherence to exercise duration is determined as the adherence to the predefined intervals/minutes of the exercise training. Reasons for non-adherence are also obtained. Adherence to exercise intensity is determined as the adherence to the prescribed intensity of the exercise training. Reasons for non-adherence are also obtained. Exercise intensity (absolute workload \[W\], relative intensity \[% of MAP, % of MPO6\], the level of dyspnoea and leg fatigue \[0-10, arbitrary units\] on the Borg CR10 scale and perceived exertion \[6-20, arbitrary units\] on the Borg Rating of RPE scale.
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Adherence to exercise duration and intensity

outcomes.description: Participant satisfaction with the performed exercise training (supramaximal HIIT / MICT) will be recorded by adaptation of an existing patient satisfaction questionnaire previously used cycling exercises in COPD. (Evans et. al. Ann Am Thorac Soc 2015)
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Satisfaction

outcomes.description: Affective response/mood will be measured using the Feeling scale, during and after exercise sessions. The Feeling scale ranges from -5 to +5, where a higher score indicates a better feeling.
outcomes.measure: Feasibility of interventions: Affective responses

outcomes.description: Adverse events are rated into four different categories: 1) minor and temporary, 2) serious symptoms (potential risk of severe injury or life threatening, 3) manifest injury or disease, and 4) death, as previously described. An adverse event rate will be calculated for each participant as the total number of sessions during which any adverse events occurred divided by the total number of attended sessions.
outcomes.measure: Adverse events

outcomes.description: Face-to-face interviews will explore the participants' experiences and perceptions of participating in the program.
outcomes.measure: Experiences of exercising and its effects

outcomes.description: Number of hospitalisations per participant during the study period. Time, cause, length of stay, and emergency room visits (with no hospitalization afterwards) and their cause will also be extracted. Hospitalizations and emergency room visits will be classified as respiratory or non-respiratory. In Phase 2, data on hospitalizations will be extracted from the participant's medical record and cross-checked with the participant's diary.
outcomes.measure: Hospitalisations

outcomes.description: Number of deaths during the study period will be extracted from the participant's medical record. Time and cause of each death will also be extracted.
outcomes.measure: Mortality

outcomes.description: In the COPD groups, number of exacerbations during the whole study period will be recorded during the whole study period. In Phase 2, data on exacerbations will be extracted from the participant's medical record and cross-checked with the participant's diary.
outcomes.measure: Exacerbations

outcomes.description: Baseline global cognitive function, as determined by the Z-score derived from CANTAB and TMT-test battery (primary outcome) will be compared between the groups at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls).
outcomes.measure: Baseline global cognitive function

outcomes.description: Baseline cardiorespiratory fitness will be compared between the groups at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Measured as maximum oxygen uptake (VO2peak \[ml O2/min/kg\]) during a standardized ramp-protocol cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) on a cycle ergometer.
outcomes.measure: Baseline cardiorespiratory fitness

outcomes.description: Baseline cardiorespiratory fitness will be compared between the groups at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Peak power (Nm/s) assessed during a seated leg extension in a dymanometer (Biodex System 4).
outcomes.measure: Baseline muscle power

outcomes.description: Baseline brain structured assessed in MRI will be compared between the groups to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Volume (mm3), area (mm2) and cortical thickness (mm) will be the unit of measure.
outcomes.measure: Baseline brain structure

outcomes.description: Baseline neuroinflammation assessed in PET/CT will be compared between the groups to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Neuroinflammation is measured as uptake rate (ki) of 11C-deprenyl in the brain assessed
outcomes.measure: Baseline neuroinflammation

outcomes.description: Baseline cognitive function assessed with the MoCA will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD vs healthy controls) and any differences in cognitive impairment at baseline. The MoCA evaluates multiple domains of cognitive function and yields a score, 0-30 points, where higher is better.
outcomes.measure: Baseline cognitive function: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)

outcomes.description: Neurotrophic factors will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healhy controls). Levels of BDNF, irisin, IGF-1, Cathepsin B and clusterin in venous blood samples. Unit of measure is pq/ml
outcomes.measure: Baseline neurotrophic factors

outcomes.description: Markers of systemic inflammation at baseline will be investigated to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Levels of interleukin-6, interleukin-8 and TNF-alpha in venous blood, measured in pq/mL, will be assessed.
outcomes.measure: Baseline inflammatory markers

outcomes.description: Baseline chronic inflammation, assessed as hs-CRP (mg/L) will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls)
outcomes.measure: Baseline chronic inflammation

outcomes.description: Baseline fibrinogen levels (g/L) will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls).
outcomes.measure: Baseline fibrinogen

outcomes.description: Baseline lactate (mmol/L) will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls).
outcomes.measure: Baseline resting lactate

outcomes.description: Proportion of slow and fast subtypes of contractile myosin heavy chain isoforms will be assessed at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). The tissue sample obtained from the vastus lateralis muscle will be examined with immunohistochemistry techniques to categorize fiber types. Expressed as relative distribution in percent and relative area of the muscle in percent.
outcomes.measure: Baseline proportion of slow and fast subtypes of contractile myosin heavy chain isoforms

outcomes.description: mRNA and protein levels of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 (PGC-1) alpha and PGC-1beta will be investigated at baseline to compare the different cohorts (COPD versus healthy controls). Unit of measure is fold-change or arbitrary units.

abstract:
Blood clots remain a serious cause of illness and death. Long-term treatment and prevention of these clots with blood thinners is often limited by bleeding risk, drug interactions, and daily dosing, leading many patients to stop treatment early. Both cancer and chemotherapy further increase the risk of clot formation.

Vortosiran is an injectable therapy that lowers Factor XI (one of the body's natural clotting helpers) production in the liver, leading to a strong and long-lasting reduction in blood clotting activity with less risk of bleeding compared to current available treatments. Studies conducted so far have shown that vortosiran is safe and shows a dose-dependent Factor XI suppression (that is, a higher dose results in a higher level of suppression) that lasts for several months, supporting testing using a limited number of injections in patients who are at higher risk of blod clot formation.

This study aims to study how safe and effective vortosiran is in patients who have had blood clots in the past and in cancer patients who are at high risk of developing blood clots.

description:
Venous thromboembolism, encompassing DVT and PE, is a common condition with a durable risk of recurrence after completion of initial therapy with systemic anticoagulation. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of patients with a first unprovoked VTE who completed at least 3 months of anticoagulant therapy and then discontinued treatment, the cumulative incidence of recurrent VTE was approximately 10% in the first year, 25% at 5 years, and 36% at 10 years, with recurrent events carrying measurable case fatality (Khan et al, 2019). Decisions about extended therapy are frequently individualized because continued anticoagulation reduces VTE recurrence but also exposes patients to ongoing bleeding risk, treatment burden, and complexity of care.

Venous thromboembolism, including in patients with cancer and chemotherapy, remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Despite effective anticoagulants, long-term management is constrained by clinically meaningful bleeding risk, drug-drug interactions with anticoagulation therapy, and the need for continuous dosing and adherence. Furthermore, many patients discontinue therapy when they perceive recurrence risk to be moderate or when bleeding risk, treatment burden, or patient preference argues against indefinite anticoagulation. These combined factors constitute an unmet need for a convenient strategy that can reduce recurrent VTE risk with a lower risk of bleeding.

Vortosiran is a subcutaneously administered siRNA designed to selectively inhibit hepatic synthesis of FXI, resulting in robust and durable suppression of FXI activity. FXI inhibition is novel and innovative anti-thrombotic strategy inhibiting blood clot formation by the intrinsic pathway without interfering with hemostatic control through the extrinsic and commen clotting pathways. Thereby reducing blood clot formation and VTE without increasing the risk of bleeding compared to current available anti-coagulant treatments.

This Phase II trial is designed to establish dose-related FXI suppression, characterize safety with repeated dosing, and generate an initial signal on clinical outcomes in two VTE prevention settings.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group Phase II trial will be conducted in two cohorts. Cohort A and Cohort B are independently enrolled and randomized. Participants are randomized (2:2:1) to low-dose vortosiran, high-dose vortosiran, or matched placebo, with dosing on Day X and Day Y and follow-up through Week 56. This trial aims to evaluate vortosiran in two complementary populations where FXI suppression could provide clinically relevant benefit and where the risk-benefit of conventional anticoagulation is often challenging.

* Cohort A (post-VTE, with participants judged to be at equipoise for extended therapy): Participants have completed 3 to 12 months of standard anticoagulation for symptomatic proximal DVT and/or PE as originally prescribed, and have had no recurrence during that initial treatment period. The cohort is restricted to patients for whom discontinuation of anticoagulation is consistent with local standard of care and where there is true equipoise about extended therapy vs only follow-up and observation.
* Cohort B (active cancer; high VTE risk): Ambulatory patients initiating a new course of systemic chemotherapy and with intermediate to high VTE risk (Khorana score ≥2), but no history of prior VTE.

abstract: Abdominal obesity is a major risk factor for metabolic disorders. Human genetic and transcriptomic studies have identified the inhibin beta E subunit (INHBE), a liver-enriched gene encoding activin E, as a potential regulator of body fat distribution and metabolic homeostasis. These findings highlight INHBE as a potential therapeutic target for RNA interference (RNAi)-based interventions. This study aimed to design and evaluate INHBE-targeting siRNAs. This was done by first using chemically synthesized siRNAs as a reference, followed by the establishment of an enzymatic in vitro transcription (IVT) workflow for siRNA synthesis and comparison of the gene-silencing efficiency of chemically synthesized and enzymatically synthesized siRNAs in human hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cells. Gene-silencing efficiency was assessed by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) to quantify INHBE mRNA expression. Among the eight candidates, siRNA-3 and siRNA-6 produced the strongest inhibitory effects on INHBE knockdown. However, chemically synthesized siRNAs produced more consistent and reproducible knockdown effects, whereas IVT synthesized-siRNAs showed greater variability across experiments. In conclusion, the dataset includes the siRNA target sequences and corresponding INHBE expression data, providing a resource for comparing siRNA candidates and evaluating the effects of target-site selection on INHBE silencing.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) can enable efficient delivery of mRNA for gene editing, making LNPs a promising vector for therapeutic treatment of inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs). Currently, LNP targeting of photoreceptors is inefficient and inconsistent between different cargos. We aimed to mimic the photoreceptor tropism of viral vectors by attaching adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid surface peptide derivatives to LNPs. We identified the most promising AAV capsid-derived peptides for photoreceptor uptake by confocal microscopy of retinal cross-sections. We generated LNP variants by surface conjugation of top performing peptides to maleimide-polyethylene glycol (PEG)-lipids. Peptide-conjugated LNPs delivered mRNA to photoreceptors and retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) in mice, with GS4, a peptide derived from the AAV9 capsid, as the top performer. Subretinal delivery of 1.0% peptide conjugated GS4-LNPs encapsulating Cre mRNA shows an 8.7-fold increase in photoreceptor transfection in the treated area compared to standard LNPs, respectively. However, when GS4-LNPs encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and sgAi9 editing was restricted to the RPE, reaching 10.9% editing of the total RPE and 31.3% editing within the treated area. Our novel GS4-LNP formulation demonstrates the feasibility for AAV peptide conjugation to LNPs and illuminates the bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors across mRNA payloads.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy shows limited efficacy in solid tumors, partly owing to poorly defined tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms. Here we show that the epigenetic regulator BAZ2A drives resistance to CD70-targeted CAR-T therapy by reprogramming tumor lipid metabolism. Using an in vivo CRISPR screen in a mouse renal cell carcinoma model, we identify BAZ2A as a key mediator that promotes the production and accumulation of palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid in the tumor microenvironment. Excess palmitic acid is taken up by CAR-T cells and impairs mitochondrial fitness by inhibiting PGC-1α activity, thereby enforcing a dysfunctional state. Pharmacologic inhibition of BAZ2A reduces lipid accumulation and restores CAR-T cell activity in vivo. These findings reveal an epigenetic-metabolic mechanism of immune resistance and suggest that targeting tumor lipid remodeling represents a therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR-T resistance in solid tumors.

title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion.

abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1 , finding ∼50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2 -related disorders.

abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1 -loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a (ARF) perturbastion altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten - and Rb1 -deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo .

title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment.

abstract: Acquired resistance to temozolomide (TMZ) constitutes a formidable clinical barrier in the management of glioblastoma (GBM). GBM organoid models (GBO) that faithfully mirror the parental tumor phenotype serve as powerful research instruments to overcome the limitations in this field. We established GBOs derived from primary glioma patients and their TMZ low-sensitivity counterparts. To unravel the intricate molecular underpinnings of this process, we performed an unbiased, integrated multi-omics analysis encompassing epigenomic, 3D genomic, and transcriptomic profiling, coupled with dual CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screening of TMZ-induced enhancers (TiEns) and their cognate target genes. Our findings demonstrate that enhancer-mediated 3D chromatin remodeling drives chemosensitivity predominantly by transcriptionally activating drug-sensitivity-associated genes, such as RasGRP3, VEGFA, BTN3A2, etc. Knockdown or knockout of these genes and enhancers renders glioma cells more sensitive to TMZ, especially RasGRP3. Our work unveils a druggable "enhancer-chromatin-target" signaling axis and proposes a novel combinatorial therapeutic strategy to surmount TMZ low sensitivity in GBM.

title: Chromatin Remodeling of RasGRP3 Underlies Temozolomide Sensitivity in Glioblastoma Organoids.

abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients supporting numerous cellular processes in normal and neoplastic cells, yet PUFA-containing phospholipids predispose cells to ferroptosis. How cancer cells from various lineages or genetic backgrounds proliferate in the presence of PUFA remains poorly understood. Here, by systematically profiling various fatty acids using a barcoded and pooled cancer cell line library, we show that a subset of cell lines is sensitive to PUFA treatment at concentrations comparable to physiological levels. We demonstrate that PUFA treatment alone is sufficient to induce ferroptosis in these cell lines that are also vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition. By correlating patterns of PUFA sensitivity with cancer cell line features including basal mRNA transcript levels, we show that PUFA sensitivity is positively associated with fatty acid binding protein 1 (FABP1) expression. Additionally, by profiling a diverse collection of fatty acids and analogs, we find that ferroptosis in cancer cells can be effectively induced by conjugated linolenic acids, in addition to PUFAs containing 1,4-pentadiene groups. Genome-wide CRISPR modifier screens in the PUFA-sensitive ES2 cells reveal a pro-ferroptosis pathway defined by enzymes that convert PUFAs to membrane-associated phospholipids, and an anti-ferroptosis pathway that segregates PUFAs by delivering them to lipid droplets. Together, we present the first comprehensive data set of PUFA-induced ferroptosis sensitivity in a collection of 554 cell lines from 19 primary lineages and suggest a potential therapeutic avenue to induce tumor cell ferroptosis using dietary metabolites.

title: Pooled Screening of Cancer Cell Lines Identifies Vulnerability to Polyunsaturated Fatty-Acid-Induced Ferroptosis.

abstract: Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

abstract: Vγ9Vδ2 T cells mediate HLA-independent targeting of tumor cells, offering unique opportunities for cancer immunotherapy, yet their therapeutic efficacy remains limited. Here, using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) as a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint that restricts Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing. GALE is a key nucleotide-sugar metabolic enzyme that controls the interconversion of UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, thereby supporting protein glycosylation and cell-surface glycan remodeling. Mechanistically, GALE promotes complex N-glycosylation of CD155 and CEACAM1, favoring their engagement with the inhibitory receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, while limiting CD155 binding to the activating receptor CD226. GALE loss potentiates Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated tumor killing in multiple mouse models and colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. Together, these findings reveal how nucleotide-sugar metabolism shapes tumor-immune communication through complex N-glycan remodeling and identify GALE and its downstream receptor-ligand interactions as potential therapeutic targets for enhancing Vγ9Vδ2 T cell antitumor activity.

abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target.

abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by dysregulation of the intestinal immune system, in which functional abnormalities of phagocytes such as macrophages play a critical role in pathogenesis. Although conventional therapies such as anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies are widely used in clinical practice, they have limitations including low response rates and significant side effects, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, macrophage-directed immunotherapy has emerged as a cutting-edge approach for IBD treatment by reprogramming intestinal phagocytes to restore immune homeostasis. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on the M1/M2 polarization framework, this review integrates recent single-cell discoveries of novel macrophage subsets (e.g. SPP1+ and TREM2+ macrophages), systematically examines the crosstalk among signaling, epigenetic, and metabolic regulatory layers, and critically evaluates translational barriers from preclinical models to clinical application. By evaluating preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the potential and challenges of these strategies. Through in-depth analysis, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis for the development of more precise and effective immunotherapies for IBD and to point out future research directions. (Literature search: PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase; January 2000-December 2025.).

abstract: Small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) often exhibit a neuroendocrine lineage identity marked by high expression of Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3). Because DLL3 shows minimal expression in normal adult tissues, it serves as an SCLC-selective tumor antigen and is the basis for clinically efficacious targeted therapies. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate DLL3 expression is therefore critical for advancing therapeutic strategies in this disease. Here, we performed transcription factor-focused and genome-wide CRISPR screens to identify regulators of DLL3 expression in SCLC. Both approaches converged on POU2F1 as a top activator of DLL3 in this tumor context. Despite its ubiquitous expression, we identify an SCLC-specific role for POU2F1 in activating DLL3 and a broader set of neuroendocrine lineage genes. Epigenomic analyses reveal tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 motifs within the DLL3 promoter that underlie the functional cooperativity between POU2F1 and the neuroendocrine master regulator ASCL1 for high-level DLL3 expression in SCLC. We provide evidence that tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 elements are part of a cis-regulatory code for the lung neuroendocrine cell fate. Together, these findings define a previously unrecognized transcriptional logic controlling DLL3 expression and establish POU2F1 as a context-specific regulator of neuroendocrine lineage in SCLC.
